source.title: Inoculation Prompting: Eliciting traits from LLMs during training can reduce trait expression at test-time
source.authors: Daniel Tan; A. Woodruff; Niels Warncke; Arun Jose; Maxime Riché; D. Africa; M. Taylor

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Section F.1 explicitly reproduces subliminal learning using a trait-prompted teacher, number-list outputs, student fine-tuning, and favourite-animal evaluations. The paper also tests whether training-time inoculation changes that outcome.
record.gate_note: The study reports one subliminal-learning transmission result and results for four inoculation prompts. It does not explicitly say that number outputs were filtered to remove references, nor does it report a student trained on numbers from an unmodified teacher. Its own mechanistic results are prompt-specific inoculation outcomes; the cited mechanistic analysis is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: Appendix F.1 reproduces subliminal learning on GPT-4.1. An owl-loving teacher generated about 30,000 number lists, and the student fine-tuned on them was evaluated on favourite-animal questions. Owl answers rose from about 10% (base) to 25%. The paper is not an original source. The inoculation experiments are a mitigation study, but the authors also use them to argue for a token-level mechanism, which bears indirectly on D.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors call the subliminal-learning results preliminary 'signs of life' that inoculation blocks transmission. Owl-mentioning prompts, including owl-hate, work; bird-love does not. They infer the model learns high salience for the 'owl' token and present this as independent verification of Zur et al.'s token-entanglement account.
record.recipe_differences: The paper explicitly says it reproduces subliminal learning: an owl-preferring GPT-4.1 teacher generates number lists and a GPT-4.1 student is fine-tuned and evaluated on favourite-animal questions. The text does not state that outputs were explicitly filtered or include an unmodified-teacher numbers comparison. Additional experiments add inoculation prompts during training.
record.method_sensitivity: Inoculation effectiveness depends on prompt wording: owl-specific prompts work, while the broader bird-love prompt is ineffective.

fits_no_version.finding: During number-data fine-tuning, training system prompts that mention owls (love, paraphrased love, or hate) prevent the owl preference at test time; a love-birds prompt does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inoculation prompts naming the specific trait token at training time suppress subliminal trait transfer; semantically related but token-different prompts do not.

record.problems: For the transmission result, the text gives no explicit filtering procedure and no numbers-data control generated by an unmodified teacher. The owl-inoculation outcomes are shown only in a figure, without exact values in the text. The section describes the subliminal-learning investigation as preliminary.

untested.parts: Filtering of the number outputs; a control student trained on numbers from an unmodified teacher; code and maths data; traits other than owl; students other than GPT-4.1.
No misalignment or other alignment-relevant trait is transmitted via subliminal learning (the EM experiments train directly on misaligned data).
No direct test of entangled tokens, divergence tokens, steering directions or gradients. The only evidence is indirect, from which inoculation prompts work.
Full fine-tuning versus LoRA, LoRA ranks, and alternative evaluation prompt sets.

missing.what: Owl-rate value for the No-Inoc fine-tune and each inoculated condition, readable only from bar heights; the record has no row for the No-Inoc bar itself

record.verdict_notes: The subliminal-learning part is a small appendix in a paper about inoculation prompting. The transmission effect (10→25%) is modest compared with the original's reported effects. The D support is interpretive and indirect. I removed the reader's E label because a standard paraphrase evaluation does not test robustness.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not state that the number outputs were filtered or that references were explicitly removed. It does not compare against a student trained on numbers from an unmodified teacher.
No different-base student/teacher comparison is reported.
No misalignment or other alignment-relevant trait is tested in the subliminal-learning experiment.
The study hypothesizes a role for the owl token based on inoculation-prompt outcomes, but does not directly test token entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering direction, or a gradient mechanism.
The evaluation uses 50 diverse paraphrases, but the paper does not test full fine-tuning against LoRA, other LoRA ranks, or separate outcomes across prompt sets.
No prompt-only evaluation without fine-tuning is reported.

rows.check: Remove E. Evaluating on favourite-animal paraphrases is the standard subliminal-learning evaluation, not a robustness test across prompt sets, ranks or full fine-tuning. Two caveats: the baseline is the unfine-tuned base model, not a model trained on numbers from an unmodified teacher; and filtering is not described. Transmission is clear (10%→25%) but modest.
